abstract_or_snippet: Full text (pdftotext-extracted, TLP:CLEAR i.e. publicly releasable). Defines IMS as 'a collection of adversarial behaviours, tools, and TTPs presumed linked to the same Threat Actor'; sets a 5-level model (political/strategic/operational/tactical/technical), NOT the 3-layer tactical/operational/strategic model cited in the project's internal secondary summary — a terminology correction for the Drafter. Two cumulative qualifying criteria: clandestinity + coordination. Worked examples: Spamouflage/Dragonbridge (PRC), Baku Initiative Group, Storm-1516/CopyCop/Lakhta, and 'Team Jorge' (Israeli private agency running IMS on behalf of paying clients, incl. anonymity-for-clients as the clandestinity criterion). Explicitly states: 'The concept of IMS is therefore applicable to any type of actor, including governmental entities, private structures, and agencies operating through shell companies.' No literal field called 'attribution_threshold' appears anywhere in the document — the internal crosslink's characterisation of it as a 'versioned, managed data-model field' is NOT substantiated by this primary text and must not be cited that way.
why_relevant: Q7: VIGINUM's own IMS definition — 5-layer model, clandestinity+coordination criteria
search_query: EU DisinfoLab Information Manipulation Set IMS framework
gate_reason: MUST ACCEPT — top-priority primary source per hard_rule ims_facts_from_primary_only; corrects two prior errors (3-layer model, attribution_threshold-as-field) and supplies the Team Jorge precedent for private-agency-as-IMS-operator that the Q7 argument's opening move depends on.

title: 1st EEAS Report on Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) Threats
abstract_or_snippet: Full text (curl+pdftotext, Feb 2023). Analyses 100 FIMI incidents / 616 involved channels (2022); introduces a 3-category attributed-channel classification (Official/State-Controlled/State-Linked) plus a residual non-attributed category, and coins 'FIMI supply chains' to describe how unattributed channels are 'integral to the successful construction of' threat-actor distribution networks — the lineage ancestor of the 4-category Exposure Matrix in the 3rd report (c054). China: 56% of Chinese-attributed incidents aim to promote a positive image; only 38 of 616 total channels attributed to China vs 207 to Russia.

title: 3rd EEAS Report on Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) Threats — Exposing the Architecture of FIMI Operations
abstract_or_snippet: FULL TEXT obtained this round via curl+pdftotext (the file is 10.7MB; round 1's WebFetch hit the 10MB cap and substituted the landing page — see c012). Two load-bearing finds: (1) the FIMI Exposure Matrix — 4 categories (Official State/State-Controlled/State-Linked/State-Aligned, the last two 'hidden connections') built on a 'behaviour-first' methodology, explicitly NOT a literal 'attribution_threshold' field but a graded connection-to-threat-actor classification; (2) an entire section 'Chinese FIMI activities using Public Relations companies' (Fig. 9) naming Shanghai Haixun Technology and Shenzhen Haimaiyunxiang Media (Haimai) as 'influence-for-hire' PR-firm intermediaries running the HaiEnergy (72-316 sites) and Paperwall (123 sites) campaigns, describing intermediaries as 'facilitators between PR firms and the inauthentic websites... either content providers or dissemination vehicles' -- with one incident (the 'VN network') directly targeting Taiwan, republishing a Global Times article framing President Lai's 2024 Double Tenth speech as provocative. Haixun/Haimai closely match NSB's named contractors '海訊社/海賣' (c010) — independent 3rd-source cross-corroboration.

title: Assessing cost-effectiveness: responses to the Doppelganger operation
author_or_org: Raquel Miguel, Maria Giovanna Sessa & Alexandre Alaphilippe (EU DisinfoLab)
abstract_or_snippet: Published 2024-05-24. This IS the 'SDA案例' precedent named in the internal crosslink. Scores five response categories (situational awareness, capability impact, triggering new responses, attribution, deterrence) against Doppelganger/SDA countermeasures. Finding: EU/US sanctions on SDA/Struktura as direct actors did not stop the operation ('the Doppelganger infrastructure remains resilient'); domain-registry and hosting-provider intermediary actions (UDRP domain seizures, deplatforming) were more disruptive than sanctions alone: 'engaging with domain name registries as the intermediary closest to the problem of impersonation is the most effective way to address issues.'
why_relevant: Q7: Doppelganger evaluation — intermediary action beat sanctioning direct actors
search_query: EU DisinfoLab Doppelganger sanctions intermediaries limited effect report
gate_reason: central empirical precedent for Q7's reaction-gap argument and the closing three-part argument (part ii, relationship-graph case for durability).

title: From Darknet to Disinfo: How a 'Bulletproof' Russian Host Evades EU Sanctions
abstract_or_snippet: Published 2025-12-04. Aeza publicly markets itself as serving 'any customer interested in its services, whether Russian, Western, or Ukrainian.'

title: Attributing Information Influence Operations: Identifying Those Responsible for Malicious Behaviour Online
author_or_org: James Pamment & Victoria Smith (NATO StratCom COE / Hybrid CoE), Riga, July 2022
abstract_or_snippet: Full text (curl+pdftotext). Systematic study of how platforms, governments and researchers assign confidence levels to attribution claims before triggering responses (takedowns, sanctions, expulsions); surveys public attribution statements and finds inconsistent or absent confidence-level disclosure across cases ('did not explicitly state a confidence level at all'). Frames the core dilemma as: without a graded, disclosed evidentiary standard, responses proportionate to confidence cannot be designed or defended.

title: If at first you don't succeed: Reflections on a rejected Art. 40 DSA data access request
abstract_or_snippet: Published 2026-03-12. First-person account of a TikTok Art.40 data-access application (on content-monetization's influence on political discourse, framed around the 2024 Romanian presidential election) rejected on 5 of 7 criteria — failure to prove vetted-researcher status, insufficient independence-from-commercial-interest showing, inadequate security/confidentiality plan, unclear data/timeframe justification, unclear publication plan. Identifies the gap as structural: Art.40 is 'a formal administrative procedure governed by specific national law' requiring institutional legal/DPO/infosec support beyond individual-researcher capacity, and its publication restrictions on sensitive findings conflict with normal academic incentives.
why_relevant: Q7: documented, named Art.40 access-request rejection — spec-vs-enforcement gap
search_query: DSA Article 40 researcher data access implementation 2026 rejected request
gate_reason: think tank (DSA Observatory), dated case; direct evidence the legal access right doesn't translate into actual access.

title: Auditing Meta and TikTok Research API Data Access under Article 40(12) of the Digital Services Act
author_or_org: Luka Bekavac & Simon Mayer (University of St. Gallen)
abstract_or_snippet: Posted 2025-06-05. Reconstructs the complete public information environment of TikTok's For You feed (US election period, July-Nov 2024) and Instagram's Explore feed (German election, Jan-Feb 2025) via sockpuppet accounts (4,000+ posts, 200+ hours), then compares against what the official Research APIs return. Quantified gaps: TikTok Research API surfaces only ~75% of user-visible posts and 17% of visible metadata parameters; Instagram ~50% of posts and 42% of metadata; ephemeral/live content 0% accessible by design; 17.7-23.3% of posts vanish (deleted) within weeks of the audit window. Conclusion: DSA-mandated data access 'risks becoming procedurally satisfied but substantively weakened.'
why_relevant: Q7: quantified DSA Art.40 shortfall — TikTok API surfaces about 75% of posts

gate_reason: preprint but rich quantified data; the strongest single quantified enforcement-gap evidence in the corpus.

title: Global pricing reveals a thriving underground market for fake account verification
author_or_org: Jon Roozenbeek, Anton Dek & Sander van der Linden (Cambridge Social Decision-Making Lab); published in Science, 2025-12-11
abstract_or_snippet: Launches the Cambridge Online Trust and Safety Index (COTSI), tracking real-time SMS-verification prices for fake-account creation across 500+ platforms and 197 countries (e.g. Russia $0.08, UK $0.10, US $0.26 vs. Japan $4.93, Australia $3.24 — inversely correlated with SIM-registration/ID-requirement strength). Across 61 elections studied, Telegram and WhatsApp verification prices spike (+12%/+15%) in pre-election periods. Proposes SIM-registration policy as a governance 'choke point' for the account-supply layer of the manipulation economy.
